subject: Medieval History
sub_topic: Foundation and dynasties — Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, Aravidu

concepts.name: Foundation of Vijayanagara: Harihara I and Bukka I — Competing Theories
key_dimensions: The Vidyaranya-inspiration legend vs. historical evidence of foundational agency
Role of the Kampili kingdom as a predecessor state and its collapse under Delhi Sultanate pressure
Debate over whether founders were previously in service of the Kakatiya/Hoysala kingdoms or the Delhi Sultanate
UPSC trap: Distinguishing between Harihara I as first ruler vs. Bukka I as the consolidator who expanded the empire

concepts.name: Role of Vidyaranya (Madhavacharya) in the Founding of Vijayanagara
key_dimensions: Spiritual and ideological patronage vs. actual political agency — extent of Vidyaranya's real influence
Sringeri Matha connection and the legitimizing role of Shaiva/Advaita Vedanta tradition
UPSC trap: Vidyaranya is often confused with Sayana (his brother), who was the Vedic commentator
The 'Hindu reaction' thesis — whether Vijayanagara was founded as a bulwark against Islam (Sewell's view) vs. a political state like any other

concepts.name: Sangama Dynasty: Chronology, Rulers, and Key Achievements
key_dimensions: Sequence of rulers: Harihara I → Bukka I → Harihara II → Bukka II → Devaraya I → Devaraya II (Deva Raya II) — commonly confused order
Devaraya II (Immadi Devaraya) as the most powerful Sangama ruler: military campaigns, incorporation of Muslim soldiers and horses
Abdur Razzaq's account of Vijayanagara during Devaraya II's reign — primary source significance
UPSC trap: Distinguishing Devaraya I (built a dam across the Tungabhadra) from Devaraya II (the greatest Sangama king)

concepts.name: Devaraya II and His Military-Administrative Innovations
key_dimensions: Recruitment of Muslims in the army and adoption of Turkish cavalry tactics — religious pragmatism over orthodoxy
Horse import problem and efforts to counter Bahmani superiority in cavalry
Abdur Razzaq's embassy description: city layout, prosperity, market descriptions — use as a primary source in UPSC answers
Literary patronage: Devaraya II himself composed in Telugu and Kannada — overlap with cultural history

concepts.name: Saluva Narasimha and the 'Saluva Usurpation' — First Dynastic Transition
key_dimensions: Context of Sangama decline: weak successors after Devaraya II, internal rebellions, and Bahmani pressure
Nature of the transition — Saluva Narasimha as a powerful nayaka/general who stepped in to 'save' the empire (not a simple coup)
UPSC trap: The Saluva dynasty was very short-lived (only two rulers) — Saluva Narasimha and his son Immadi Narasimha
Concept of 'protective usurpation' and how it set a precedent for the Tuluva transition

concepts.name: Tuluva Dynasty: Foundation by Vira Narasimha and the Role of Narasa Nayaka
key_dimensions: Narasa Nayaka as the real power behind the throne during late Saluva period — 'kingmaker' role
Vira Narasimha's seizure of power from Immadi Narasimha — second dynastic transition and its justification
UPSC trap: Narasa Nayaka (father) is sometimes confused with Vira Narasimha (son who actually founded the Tuluva dynasty)
Tuluva origins — the Tulu-speaking coastal Karnataka region and its significance

concepts.name: Krishnadevaraya: Reign, Military Conquests, and Political Significance
key_dimensions: Key military victories: defeat of the Gajapati kingdom of Orissa (Battle of Udayagiri, 1512; capture of Raichur, 1520), campaigns against Bahmani successor states
UPSC trap: Krishnadevaraya defeated the Gajapatis AND recovered Raichur from Bijapur — two different campaigns often confused
Treaty of friendship with the Portuguese and its strategic significance for horse trade
Title 'Kannada Rajya Rama Ramana' and 'Andhra Bhoja' — their linguistic and cultural implications

concepts.name: Krishnadevaraya as a Literary Figure: Amuktamalyada and Ashtadiggajas
key_dimensions: Amuktamalyada: written in Telugu, a devotional-political text — its themes of ideal kingship and Vaishnavism
The Ashtadiggajas (Eight Elephants): the eight poets in his court — Allasani Peddana as 'Andhra Kavita Pitamaha' (grandfather of Telugu poetry) and his work Manucharitra
UPSC trap: Krishnadevaraya wrote in Telugu, NOT Kannada, despite ruling from Karnataka — a frequent confusion point
Distinction between Krishnadevaraya's own compositions and works patronized by him

concepts.name: Vijayanagara–Bahmani Conflict: Structural Causes and Key Battles
key_dimensions: Three structural causes of conflict: control of the Raichur Doab (fertile land between Krishna and Tungabhadra), control of the port of Goa for horse trade, and rivalry over the Tungabhadra-Krishna delta
Battle of Raichur (1520) under Krishnadevaraya — a decisive Vijayanagara victory but ultimately not permanent
UPSC trap: The Bahmani kingdom fragmented into five Deccan Sultanates — Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Berar, Bidar, Golconda — and it was the COMBINED force of these that defeated Vijayanagara at Talikota
Role of Portuguese alliance in the horse trade equation

concepts.name: Battle of Talikota (1565): Causes, Course, and Consequences
key_dimensions: UPSC trap on naming: Also called 'Battle of Bannihatti' or 'Rakshasi-Tangadi' — the actual battle site was NOT Talikota; UPSC has tested this
Coalition of Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar) vs. Vijayanagara under Aliya Rama Raya
Role of treachery: Two Muslim commanders in Vijayanagara's army switched sides during battle
Consequence: Destruction/sacking of Hampi, end of Vijayanagara as a major power — but the empire did NOT end in 1565 (continued under Aravidu dynasty)

concepts.name: Aliya Rama Raya: Power, Administration, and Role in Deccan Politics
key_dimensions: Aliya Rama Raya as the de facto ruler during the reign of Sadashiva Raya (last Tuluva ruler) — regent who held real power
His policy of playing Deccan Sultanates against each other — interventionist Deccan diplomacy
UPSC trap: Aliya Rama Raya was a son-in-law of Krishnadevaraya (Aliya = son-in-law in Telugu/Kannada), not a blood member of the Tuluva dynasty
His death at Talikota as the turning point — the empire's collapse was largely personal to his leadership

concepts.name: Aravidu Dynasty: Post-Talikota Survival and Decline
key_dimensions: UPSC trap: The Vijayanagara Empire did NOT end at Talikota in 1565 — it continued under the Aravidu dynasty until c. 1646
Capital shift from Hampi to Penugonda and later to Chandragiri — significance for political geography
Tirumala as the founder of the Aravidu dynasty — his relationship to Aliya Rama Raya
Fragmentation into the Nayaka kingdoms (Madurai, Tanjavur, Ikkeri, Gingee) — the Nayaka system as a legacy of Vijayanagara administration

concepts.name: The Nayankara/Nayaka System: Administrative Structure and Its Significance
key_dimensions: Nayaka system as a form of military feudalism: nayakas received land grants (amaram) in exchange for military service and revenue remittance
Distinction between Nayakas as governors vs. later independent Nayaka kingdoms (Madurai Nayakas, Tanjavur Nayakas) — the evolution from office to dynasty
UPSC trap: The Nayaka system is often compared to the iqta system of the Delhi Sultanate — key differences: no rotation, more hereditary tendency, tied to specific military quotas
Role of the system in the empire's eventual fragmentation

concepts.name: Religious Policy of Vijayanagara: Composite Character vs. 'Hindu Kingdom' Label
key_dimensions: Rulers were primarily Shaiva or Vaishnava but patronized all sects including Jainism; Krishnadevaraya was a Vaishnava but respected Shaiva traditions

UPSC trap: Vijayanagara is often called a 'Hindu kingdom' set up against Muslims, but rulers employed Muslims, traded with Muslim powers, and fought Hindu kingdoms (Gajapatis, Odisha) just as frequently
The Vitthala temple and Hazara Rama temple at Hampi as examples of royal religious patronage
Contrast with Bahmani/Deccan Sultanate religious policies — useful for comparative questions

concepts.name: Foreign Accounts of Vijayanagara: Abdur Razzaq, Nicolo Conti, Domingo Paes, Fernao Nuniz
key_dimensions: Abdur Razzaq (Persian, visited during Devaraya II, 1443): description of the city's grandeur, market, and administration
Nicolo Conti (Italian, c. 1420): earliest foreign account, description of the city's size — 'as large as Rome'
Domingo Paes (Portuguese, visited during Krishnadevaraya): eyewitness to the Mahanavami festival, description of the king
UPSC trap: Fernao Nuniz visited AFTER Krishnadevaraya during the reign of Achyuta Raya — not a contemporary of Krishnadevaraya; the two Portuguese accounts are frequently confused

concepts.name: Vijayanagara Capital Hampi: Urban Layout, Monuments, and UNESCO Status
key_dimensions: Hampi declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986 — 'Group of Monuments at Hampi'
Key structures: Vitthala Temple (with the famous stone chariot and musical pillars), Virupaksha Temple, Lotus Mahal, Elephant Stables, Hazara Rama Temple
UPSC trap: The Virupaksha Temple at Hampi predates the Vijayanagara Empire and was a local Shaiva shrine that the rulers adopted and expanded — it was NOT built by Vijayanagara rulers
Urban planning features: royal enclosure, sacred center, urban core — as described by historians like Noboru Karashima and Burton Stein

concepts.name: Sangama to Saluva to Tuluva Transitions: Pattern of Dynastic Change
key_dimensions: All three transitions followed a similar pattern: weak central ruler → powerful military commander steps in → new dynasty established with legitimizing narrative
UPSC trap: None of the transitions involved complete outsiders — Saluva Narasimha was a nayaka of Vijayanagara, Narasa Nayaka/Vira Narasimha were commanders within the system
How each transition was 'justified' ideologically — concept of 'protecting the kingdom' as a legitimizing tool
Contrast with Mughal succession pattern (which involved wars of succession among princes)

concepts.name: Vijayanagara and the Portuguese: Trade, Diplomacy, and the Horse Trade
key_dimensions: Strategic importance of Portuguese-controlled Goa for importing Arabian/Persian horses — a military necessity given the Deccan terrain
Krishnadevaraya's friendly relations with the Portuguese vs. later strained relations under Achyuta Raya
UPSC trap: Vijayanagara sought Portuguese alliance primarily for HORSES and to counter Bijapur's control of Goa — NOT primarily for trade goods or Christian missionary purposes
The horse trade as a structural factor in Vijayanagara's military capability — connects to broader question of why Indian kingdoms depended on imported horses

concepts.name: Harihara II and Bukka II: Consolidation of the Sangama Dynasty
key_dimensions: Harihara II's long reign and significant territorial expansion — brought most of South India under Vijayanagara suzerainty
UPSC trap: Harihara II (second generation) is often confused with Harihara I (founder) — key difference: Harihara I founded the empire, Harihara II greatly expanded it
Relation with the declining Bahmani kingdom during this period — nature of conflicts and treaties
Bukka II's brief reign and its limited historical significance — useful for elimination in MCQs

concepts.name: Achyuta Raya and Sadashiva Raya: Late Tuluva Period and Imperial Decline
key_dimensions: Achyuta Raya succeeded Krishnadevaraya — a weaker ruler under whose reign Aliya Rama Raya began accumulating real power
Sadashiva Raya as the last Tuluva ruler — a puppet under Aliya Rama Raya; technically the king during the Battle of Talikota
UPSC trap: The Battle of Talikota was fought during the reign of Sadashiva Raya, but it was ALIYA RAMA RAYA (not Sadashiva) who commanded the army and was killed
Fernao Nuniz's account covers Achyuta Raya's period — source significance for this transitional phase
